issues.description: Field name mismatch for Book.title: The problem statement (and the client code) specify that the Book type has a property named `title` (a String). The solution's Book struct instead declares `let bookTitle: String` (member declared at Bookstore.swift line 26). The solution's Client and the Book initializations use `Book(title: ...)` and `book.title`, which do not match the struct's memberwise initializer or property name. This inconsistency prevents the code from compiling and confuses students about the required attribute name.
issues.suggestedFix: Rename the Book struct property from `bookTitle` to `title` (e.g. `let title: String`) so the member name matches the problem statement and all usages. Ensure the struct's memberwise initializer and all references (calls like `Book(title:..., author:..., genres: ...)` and accesses like `book.title`) compile consistently.

issues.description: The problem statement defines the Book concept with a property named `title` (problem_statement.md lines 16-18). In the solution, the Book struct declares the property as `bookTitle` (Sources/BookstoreLib/Bookstore.swift line 26), while the solution's Client code constructs and uses Book instances with `title` (Sources/BookstoreLib/Client.swift uses `Book(title: ...)` at lines 34-36 and references `book.title` at line 11). Because the same conceptual field is given different identifiers (`title` vs `bookTitle`) across artifacts, students cannot reliably map the exercise requirement (a Book with a `title` property) to the provided implementation and client usage, causing confusion and likely compilation errors.
issues.suggestedFix: Rename the Book struct property `bookTitle` to `title` in Sources/BookstoreLib/Bookstore.swift. Ensure the memberwise initializer and all references/initializers in Sources/BookstoreLib/Client.swift use `title` (e.g. `Book(title: ..., author: ..., genres: ...)` and `book.title`) so the implementation matches the problem statement and client usage.
